body: It would be great if you could also add OpenCode support.

Fixed in v2 branch. graspologic is now optional — graphify falls back to NetworkX's built-in louvain_communities if graspologic isn't installed. Install with just pip install graphifyy (no graspologic needed). For best clustering quality, pip install graphifyy[leiden] to get Leiden via graspologic.

Added a Privacy section to the README. Code files are processed locally via tree-sitter (no API calls). Docs, papers, and images are sent to the Claude API (Anthropic) using your own API key. No telemetry or tracking of any kind.

OpenCode support is now shipped in v0.3.0 — `skill-opencode.md` uses OpenCode's `@mention` syntax for parallel subagent extraction, and `graphify install --platform opencode` copies it to `.config/opencode/skills/graphify/SKILL.md`. Also added `graphify opencode install` for always-on AGENTS.md rules. Thanks for the request!

Closing — Codex, OpenCode, and OpenClaw support all shipped in v0.3.0. Each platform has its own optimized skill file and `graphify install --platform <name>` routes to the right config directory. Always-on hooks (`graphify codex/opencode/claw install`) write AGENTS.md rules for persistent graph-first behaviour.

Genuinely one of the more useful reviews I have gotten. A lot of these hit real issues.

I fixed six of them in de60b68:

The git hook was the worst one. Catching an exception and exiting 0 means git thinks everything went fine while your graph is quietly stale. That is now exit 1.

The token budget math was off by about 3x. Changed the multiplier from 4 to 3, which is closer to reality for mixed graph text output.

`_is_file_node` was doing extension matching on label strings, which would incorrectly filter a class named `config.py`. It now checks whether the label matches the actual filename from the node's `source_file` attribute.

`_node_community_map` was copy-pasted between `analyze.py` and `export.py`. Removed the duplicate, import from one place now.

Cache writes are atomic. Write to a temp file, then `os.replace()`. No more corrupt JSON on a mid-write crash.

`detect_incremental` now tracks deleted files and returns them so callers can clean up ghost nodes instead of letting them accumulate forever.

The refactoring points (extract.py size, inline JS in export.py, print vs logging, loose test assertions, magic numbers) are all valid and on the list for v0.4.0. They are real but not bugs.

On point 15, `nx.Graph()` is intentional. Leiden needs an undirected graph to run community detection. Edge direction is stored in attrs for export purposes. It is not a workaround, it is just how the clustering layer works.
yeap!

I went through all of these carefully. Here is what I fixed and where I pushed back.

**Fixed in c529e22 and 808cd98:**

`_fetch_tweet` was making a raw `urlopen` call for the oEmbed request, completely bypassing the `safe_fetch` layer everything else goes through. That is now routed through `safe_fetch_text`.

The Cypher export was only escaping single quotes. A label with a backslash before a quote would break out of the string. Added `_cypher_escape()` which escapes backslashes first, then quotes, in the right order.

Community labels were going into the HTML template via `community_name` without sanitization. Added `sanitize_label()` there.

`graph_diff` was using `(u, v, relation)` as the edge key on an undirected graph where iteration order is arbitrary. Changed to `(min(u, v), max(u, v), relation)` so diffs are stable.

Cache was keyed only on file content hash. Two files with identical content shared a cache entry, meaning the second file's nodes had the wrong `source_file` baked in. The key now includes the resolved file path.

Hook uninstall was splitting on the start marker string, which would corrupt any content after the graphify section. Replaced with paired start and end markers so removal is precise regardless of what else is in the hook file.

Watch mode was using a list for the changed set with an O(n) membership check on every filesystem event. Changed to a set.

`_rebuild_code` was reading every code file in the repo to count words on every single save event. That count is not needed during watch rebuilds so it is skipped now.

**Where I pushed back:**

On point 3, the XSS concern via `innerHTML` is not exploitable. `sanitize_label()` calls `html.escape()` which converts `<` to `<`. When that lands in `innerHTML`, the browser renders it as literal text, not markup. The escaping is not reversed by JSON parsing.

On point 15, `nx.Graph()` is intentional. Leiden community detection requires an undirected graph. Direction is preserved in edge attrs for export. This is not a workaround around the data model, it is the correct model for topology based clustering.

Good reviews both times.

Add a `.graphifyignore` file to the folder you run graphify on and it will skip anything matching your patterns. Same syntax as `.gitignore` so there is nothing new to learn.

```
# .graphifyignore
vendor/
node_modules/
dist/
*.generated.py
```

Patterns match against relative file paths, directory names, and individual path segments, so `vendor/` will catch `vendor/lib.py` wherever it sits in the tree.

I appreciate the work here but I am going to pass on this one.

graphify's design is that it runs entirely on your existing AI assistant's API key with no additional accounts or services needed. Adding Nimble as a dependency for core functionality like URL fetching changes that promise, and it ties graphify to a specific commercial vendor.

The JS rendering problem is real but I would rather solve it at the platform level (documenting that users can save content manually, or use browser extensions to export clean markdown) than by requiring a second paid API.

The proposal is well thought out and COBOL would be a genuinely useful addition given how many legacy modernization projects are out there.

One thing to check before starting: `tree-sitter-cobol` does not appear to be published on PyPI yet. All the other languages graphify supports use PyPI-published tree-sitter bindings so the PR would need to either find a published package or ship the grammar bindings. Worth confirming that exists and works before writing the extractor.

On your open questions:

Data divisions and record structures — skip them for now. The graph value is in understanding program flow and dependencies, not data layout. PROGRAM-ID, SECTIONs, PARAGRAPHs, CALL, PERFORM, and COPY already give you that. Record structures can always be added later.

Copybooks — treat them as imports. A `COPY mybook` is conceptually the same as an import in any other language. The copybook file becomes a node and the COPY statement becomes an `imports_from` edge pointing to it. That fits naturally into the existing graph model.

If you find a working PyPI package, happy to review a PR following the same pattern as the other language extractors in `extract.py`.

Good call — .docx and .xlsx are exactly the kind of files that end up in a legal corpus alongside PDFs. Adding these makes sense.

Plan for .docx: use `python-docx` to extract text and convert to markdown (preserves headings, tables, lists). For .xlsx: use `openpyxl` to read sheets and render them as markdown tables. Both would go into the existing semantic extraction pipeline — Claude reads the markdown output the same way it reads .md files today.

Will add this as an optional dependency group (`pip install graphifyy[office]`) so people who don't need it don't pull in extra packages. Tracking for a near-term release.

https://github.com/safishamsi/graphify/issues/7 would likely fix a big part of the problem, but not all of it.

If #7 is implemented as described (a post-merge local embedding pass over all nodes that adds semantically_similar_to edges), it should significantly reduce the “cross-chunk similarity edges get missed” issue, because similarity linking would become global rather than limited to “within this chunk”.

However, it would not necessarily recover other cross-chunk relationships that depend on reading the original file context, such as references, cites, rationale_for, conceptually_related_to, or chunk-scoped hyperedges. Those would still require a separate global linking / second-pass semantic step if you want high recall across chunks.

I'm excited about this issue. Semantic search as an entry point into graph traversal is the right architectural move, and I'd like to contribute.
Before I start, I have a philosophical question to confirm I'm building in the right direction.
Karpathy's original approach deliberately avoids embedding infrastructure, the idea being that if the LLM compiles the knowledge structure itself, it can navigate it by reasoning over a rich index rather than relying on vector similarity. Graphify started from that same spirit, but this issue moves toward a more traditional semantic search stack.
Is that a conscious architectural decision that Graphify is evolving into something closer to a code intelligence layer, where embeddings make sense because the graph is built mechanically (AST parsing) rather than LLM-compiled? Or is the goal to stay closer to the "LLM as librarian" model, in which case the fix might be enriching node labels and summaries at build time so the LLM can navigate without keyword matching?
I want to make sure any PR I open is moving in the right direction. I'd value your thoughts before we dive in.

Thanks for the detailed report. Reviewed the current code:

- `to_cypher()`: `_cypher_escape()` correctly handles both backslash and single-quote sequences; `ftype` and `rel` go through strict regex stripping for identifier positions
- `push_to_neo4j()`: uses parameterized queries (`$id`, `$props`, `$src`, `$tgt`) for all value positions; `ftype`/`rel` go through `_safe_label()`/`_safe_rel()`

One gap you correctly identified: `ftype` could produce a label starting with a digit after stripping, which is invalid in Cypher. Fixed in ffd8906 — now falls back to `Entity` if the sanitized string doesn't start with a letter.

Fixed in v0.3.13. Hook now outputs `{"hookSpecificOutput":{"hookEventName":"PreToolUse","additionalContext":"..."}}` so Claude receives it as a system reminder before every Glob/Grep call.

Fixed in v0.3.13. Both `type_declaration` and method receiver nodes now use `pkg_scope = path.parent.name` (the package directory) instead of the file stem. Methods on the same type across multiple files in a package now share one canonical type node, so cross-file methods are no longer orphaned.

Fixed in v0.3.13. All intermediate files (`.graphify_detect.json`, `.graphify_ast.json`, `.graphify_semantic.json`, etc.) now live inside `graphify-out/` instead of the project root. Add `graphify-out/` to your `.gitignore` to keep everything clean.

Addressed in v0.3.13:

**Issue 2 (P0 — cross-file imports crash blocking non-Python files):** Fixed. `_resolve_cross_file_imports` is now guarded with `if py_paths:` and wrapped in `try/except` so a Python parser failure can't abort extraction for Swift/ObjC/C and other languages.

**Issue 3 (P1 — PDFs in `.imageset`/`.xcassets` misclassified as papers):** Fixed. `classify_file` now checks for asset catalog directory markers in the path and returns `None` instead of `FileType.PAPER`.

The remaining issues (tree-sitter version pinning, community fragmentation on 22k-node graphs, HTML 5k cap, god-node filtering, iOS preset) are larger scope and tracked for future milestones.

Fixed in v0.3.14. `graphify codex install` now writes a PreToolUse hook to `.codex/hooks.json` in addition to AGENTS.md. The hook fires before every Bash tool call and injects the graphify reminder as `additionalContext` JSON — same mechanism as Claude Code.

Fixed in v0.3.14. The `--update` merge step now reads `deleted_files` from the incremental detection result and prunes all nodes whose `source_file` matches a deleted path before merging the new extraction. Ghost nodes are cleaned automatically on every `--update` run.

Both work well — the choice depends on your setup:

**Claude (claude-3-5-sonnet or claude-opus-4):** Best semantic extraction quality. graphify was built and tuned on Claude, so prompts and output parsing are optimized for it. Recommended for deep mode (`--mode deep`) and large corpora.

**Codex (o3, o4-mini):** Works well for code-heavy projects — strong at structural reasoning. Semantic extraction quality is slightly lower for doc/paper content but very fast. Good for code-only repos where you mostly care about AST relationships.

Bottom line: use Claude if you have access to it. Codex is a solid fallback.

Gemini isn't directly supported yet as a model provider — graphify currently uses the Anthropic SDK for semantic extraction. Adding Gemini would require a second extraction backend.

That said, if you run graphify purely for AST/structural extraction (code files only, no docs/papers/images), no LLM is used at all — the output is deterministic and free.

Gemini support is tracked as part of the v0.4.0 milestone (#7) which will add a model-agnostic extraction interface.

`tree-sitter-dart` is not yet published to PyPI, which is a hard requirement for graphify (all language bindings must be pip-installable). We'll add Dart support as soon as an official PyPI package is available. Watching the tree-sitter-dart repo for a release.

COBOL support is on our radar — the extractor design is solid (PROGRAM-ID, SECTIONs, PARAGRAPHs, CALL, PERFORM, COPY as imports). The blocker is `tree-sitter-cobol` not being available on PyPI — all graphify language bindings must be pip-installable. Will add it as soon as a published package exists.

You can use `--obsidian-dir` to write graphify output into an existing vault:

```
/graphify . --obsidian-dir /path/to/your/vault
```

This writes a `graphify/` folder inside your vault with wiki pages for every node, linked with `[[wikilinks]]` so they appear in Obsidian's graph view alongside your existing notes. Your existing vault structure is untouched — graphify only adds files, never modifies existing ones.

The best starting points for working with graphify output:

1. **`graphify-out/GRAPH_REPORT.md`** — start here. God nodes (highest-degree), community structure, surprising connections, suggested questions, and knowledge gaps. Human-readable summary of the entire graph.

2. **`graphify-out/graph.html`** — interactive visual. Click nodes, search, filter by community. Best for exploring unfamiliar codebases.

3. **`graphify-out/graph.json`** — machine-readable. Full node/edge data with confidence scores, source file references, and community IDs. Use with `graphify query` to traverse the graph without LLM cost:
   `graphify query --graph graphify-out/graph.json --dfs 'MyClass' --budget 20`

4. **`graphify-out/wiki/`** (if `--wiki` was used) — one markdown page per node, linkable from any note-taking tool.

The report + HTML cover most exploration needs. The JSON + query CLI are for agentic/programmatic workflows.

Confirmed — OpenCode's `tool.execute.before` plugin event is the right hook for this. The implementation requires a JavaScript plugin file (`.opencode/plugins/graphify.js`) and registration in `opencode.json`. We're tracking this for the next platform integration release. The AGENTS.md approach continues to work in the meantime.

Aider support is straightforward — Aider reads `CONVENTIONS.md` or `.aider.conf.yml` in the project root for persistent instructions. The graphify rules (read GRAPH_REPORT.md before answering, rebuild after changes) can go there directly. We'll add a `graphify aider install` command that writes to `CONVENTIONS.md` following the same pattern as the existing platform installs. Tracking this.

The exit code 49 in git-bash on Windows is a known issue with Claude Code running multi-line Python `-c` commands through git-bash — the shell sometimes terminates the subprocess early. Two workarounds while we investigate:

1. **Use WSL** — Claude Code runs natively in WSL and graphify works correctly there.
2. **Use the Windows skill** — `graphify install --platform windows` installs a Windows-compatible skill variant that avoids multi-line bash blocks.

We moved all intermediate files into `graphify-out/` in v0.3.13 which may also help with path-related failures. If you're still seeing it after updating to 0.3.14, please reopen with the full error output.

Really impressive engineering here, but this goes well beyond graphify's scope. Adding 46 file formats, archive extraction, YouTube transcripts, and URL crawling turns graphify into a general-purpose ingestion layer — that's a different product. graphify's strength is being focused and lean: structured extraction from code + docs + images you already have. We'll keep an eye on community interest but for now keeping the scope tight.

The refactor is well-executed and the architectural concerns you're addressing are real — extract.py is getting large. We're deliberately deferring this split until the language set stabilizes (we're adding Dart, COBOL etc. soon and the split boundary will shift). When we do it, we'll use a similar structure to what you've proposed here. Closing for now but your design is a good reference.

Thanks for reporting this. Two things are going on here.

**No graphify-out folder (pipeline not running)**

This was a bug in v0.3.17 where the skill tried to write `graphify-out/.graphify_python` before the `graphify-out/` directory existed. The write would fail silently, and every subsequent step that reads from that file would also fail, leaving only AGENTS.md from the install step. This is fixed in v0.3.18. Please upgrade and try again:

```bash
pip install --upgrade graphifyy
```

**PDF files not scanned**

PDF support is an optional dependency and is not included in the base install. To enable it:

```bash
pip install graphifyy[pdf]
```

This adds `pypdf` and `html2text` which graphify uses to extract text from PDFs before passing them to Claude for semantic extraction.

Let us know if upgrading resolves the pipeline issue.

Thanks for the detailed report. A couple of clarifications and one real fix.

**graphifyy is a real package**

It has been on PyPI since April 3rd: https://pypi.org/project/graphifyy/

The double-y is intentional while the single-y name is being reclaimed. The README explains this. It is not hallucinated and not a typosquatting risk since we own and publish it.

**The --break-system-packages concern is valid**

You are right that blindly appending --break-system-packages on a Homebrew Python environment is risky. The flag was there as a fallback for PEP 668 managed environments but the current code applies it unconditionally without trying a clean install first. We are fixing the skill to try a plain pip install first and only fall back to --break-system-packages if that fails, which is the correct behaviour. This will go out in the next release.

**The screenshot**

The agent output in your screenshot is correct behaviour from the skill. The install line it ran is what we shipped. The fix addresses the flag ordering, not the package name.

The "stale allowlist silently skipping valid files" pattern is exactly the kind of bug that traditional quality tools completely miss — and it gets worse with AI-generated code.

Here's why: AI coding agents tend to import and use newer file types/extensions that weren't in the original allowlist. The hook exits 0 (success), the graph isn't rebuilt, and the CI pipeline reports green. Nobody notices until something breaks downstream and the investigation reveals the graph was stale for weeks.

What's particularly tricky about this class of bug:

1. **Exit code 0 masks the failure**: Silent success is more dangerous than a loud error
2. **Config drift is invisible**: `CODE_EXTS` in hooks.py diverges from the authoritative `CODE_EXTENSIONS` in detect.py, and there's no CI check that enforces consistency
3. **AI agents amplify the problem**: An AI refactoring tool might rename `.js` → `.mjs` or add `.jsx` support, unaware that the post-commit hook will silently ignore these changes

The fix (canonical source of truth + sync) is correct. We handle a similar problem in CI: checking that all declared dependencies actually exist on their registries, because the alternative (silent 0 exit) leads to exactly this kind of undetected drift.

Great framing — the single-promise problem is real and it shapes everything from your GitHub star trajectory to which communities rally behind it.

**Practical recommendation: Lead with the coding-assistant story.**

Here's why it wins on GitHub:

1. **Specific > Broad in headlines.** "Turn any folder into a queryable knowledge graph" is impressive but requires explanation. "Coding assistant skill that cuts 65% of tokens" (see JuliusBrussee/caveman) got 18k stars in days because the value prop fits in one breath.

2. **Developer community is your PLG engine.** GitHub stars → GitHub Trending → HackerNews/Reddit → organic growth. Lead with what devs can *try right now*, not the grand vision.

3. **Breadth is fine — just not on the tin.** You can absolutely expand to "personal/work knowledge graph" *after* you have the dev community locked in. Figma started as a prototyping tool. The platform story came later.

**Concrete first-step:** Change the README H1 to something like:
> "**graphify** — Turn any codebase into a queryable knowledge graph. Works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and 6 other coding agents."

Then put the personal/work memory layer in the "what's next" section. Let the dev use case be the wedge.

The README describes `--watch` as:

> **Auto-sync** (`--watch`) - run in a background terminal and the graph updates itself as your codebase changes. Code file saves trigger an instant rebuild (AST only, no LLM). Doc/image changes notify you to run `--update` for the LLM re-pass.

"The graph updates itself" implies an incremental merge, consistent with how `--update` is described separately:

> `/graphify ./raw --update` - re-extract only changed files, **merge into existing graph**

But `--watch` doesn't merge. `_rebuild_code` builds a new graph from AST-only data and overwrites `graph.json` entirely. On a mixed repo (code + docs), this silently destroys all semantic nodes, INFERRED edges, hyperedges, and community labels from the prior `/graphify` run.

The distinction between `--update` (merge) and `--watch` (overwrite) is not documented and contradicts the "auto-sync" framing.

> ## Background
> Graphify currently produces a **single flat knowledge graph** — all source files are extracted, merged into one `graph.json`, and served via MCP as a flat graph. This works well for small-to-medium projects, but breaks down at scale:
> 
> 1. **Information Overload**: A 500+ file project produces thousands of nodes. LLM query token budgets are wasted on irrelevant details, and key architectural information is buried in noise.
> 2. **No Abstraction Levels**: Real-world architectures are naturally hierarchical (functions → modules → services → system). A flat graph cannot distinguish "how does auth work?" (implementation detail) from "what is the system architecture?" (high-level overview). Both questions hit the same undifferentiated graph.
> 3. **Full-Graph Search Overhead**: Every query traverses the entire graph. There's no way to narrow scope based on the question's abstraction level.
> 
> ## Proposed Solution
> Introduce **Hierarchical Knowledge Aggregation** — knowledge should be layered like geographic maps (street-level → city-level → country-level), where each upper layer contains its own content plus a summarized view of the layer below.
> 
> ### Core Concepts
> * **Layered DAG**: A `layers.yaml` config defines a strict parent-child hierarchy. Parents are built before children (topological order). No cycles, no cross-layer dependencies.
> * **Bottom-up Aggregation**: Each layer builds its own graph from its sources, then merges a summarized sub-graph from its parent. Summary nodes are prefixed with `summary:<parent_id>:` for collision avoidance and provenance tracking.
> * **Intelligent Query Routing**: Questions are automatically routed to the most appropriate layer based on keyword matching and abstraction-level heuristics. Abstract questions ("system architecture") go to upper layers; concrete questions ("function implementation") go to lower layers. Auto-zoom drills down when results are sparse.
> * **5 Aggregation Strategies**: `none` (no-op), `topk_filter` (degree-based selection), `community_collapse` (community detection → abstract nodes), `llm_summary` (LLM semantic summarization), `composite` (CC → LLM pipeline).
> 
> ### Value Proposition
> Before	After
> Single flat graph, all detail levels mixed	Layered graphs with clear abstraction boundaries
> Every query searches the full graph	Queries routed to the right abstraction level
> No way to compress/reduce graph size	5.3x compression from code layer to overview layer (validated on real data)
> No provenance for how summaries were derived	Full provenance: `aggregation/from_<parent>.json` per layer
> No structural comparison between views	`layer-diff` command for cross-layer comparison
> Sequential build only	Parallel same-depth builds with graceful fallback
> ### Validation
> Built and tested on 3 real corpora (example, httpx, mixed-corpus) with a 3-layer architecture:
> 
> L0 (Code): 266 nodes, 357 edges — raw code extraction L1 (Docs): 146 nodes, 154 edges — docs + topk_filter summary from L0 L2 (Overview): 50 nodes, 64 edges — code + community_collapse summary from L1
> 
> **5.3x node compression** from L0 → L2, with query routing correctly distinguishing abstract vs. concrete questions.
> 
> 103 unit tests + real-data integration tests, all passing.
> 
> ### Implementation (4 Phases)
> Phase	Scope	Tasks
> 1. Layer Config Foundation	`layers.yaml` parsing, DAG validation, topological sort, `LayerRegistry`	36
> 2. Aggregation Engine	5 strategies (none, topk, collapse, llm, composite) with LLM fallback	32
> 3. Query Routing	`QueryRouter`, keyword + level-weighted scoring, auto-zoom, MCP integration	27
> 4. CLI Polish	`layer-info`/`layer-tree`/`layer-diff` commands, provenance, parallel build, auto-detection	22
> **Reference**: Full design doc and test records in [`README_TEAM.md`](./README_TEAM.md) and [`README_TEAM.zh-CN.md`](./README_TEAM.zh-CN.md).
> 
> ### New CLI Commands
> graphify build --layers layers.yaml              # Build all layers
> graphify build --layers layers.yaml --layer L2   # Incremental rebuild
> graphify layer-info --layers layers.yaml         # Table of layer stats
> graphify layer-tree --layers layers.yaml         # ASCII tree
> graphify layer-diff L0 L1 --layers layers.yaml   # Cross-layer comparison
> graphify query "architecture?" --layers layers.yaml  # Auto-routed query
> graphify query "auth function" --layer L0        # Direct layer query
> ### New MCP Tools
> * `layer_info` — List all layers with stats
> * `drill_down` — Query a specific layer by ID
> * `query_graph` — Auto-routed query (multi-layer mode, auto-detected)
> 
> ### Backward Compatibility
> 100% backward compatible. Without `--layers`, Graphify behaves exactly as before — single flat graph, no changes to existing workflows. Multi-layer mode is opt-in via `layers.yaml`.

A useful clarification from local testing:

When `graspologic` is installed, `matplotlib` is also installed transitively, so the SVG export path can appear to work even though `graphify` does not declare `matplotlib` itself.

That does not remove the packaging issue here. `graspologic` is an optional dependency, so its presence is not guaranteed for users who want SVG export. As a result, `graphify` currently relies on an indirect dependency for a direct feature in `graphify.export.to_svg()`.

That coupling is also not intuitive from a user perspective. SVG export and Leiden clustering are separate features, and users should not need to install `graspologic` just to make `--svg` work.

The packaging contract would be clearer if `matplotlib` were declared explicitly for the SVG export path, rather than being satisfied only incidentally when `graspologic` happens to be installed.

The video description undersells it a bit — graphify is not primarily a graph visualizer, the HTML/SVG output is just one of several outputs.

What graphify actually does:

**It turns any folder of files into a queryable knowledge graph that your AI assistant uses automatically.**

The full pipeline:
1. **Structural extraction** — deterministic AST pass over code files (classes, functions, imports, call graphs, rationale comments) with no LLM needed. 23 languages supported.
2. **Semantic extraction** — parallel AI subagents extract concepts, relationships, citations, and design rationale from docs, papers, and images.
3. **Community detection** — Leiden algorithm clusters the graph into named communities (e.g. "Attention Mechanism", "Training Pipeline").
4. **Three outputs** — interactive HTML viz, GraphRAG-ready `graph.json`, and a plain-language `GRAPH_REPORT.md` audit report with god nodes and surprising connections.

The real value is the **always-on assistant integration**, not the visualization:

- A **PreToolUse hook** fires before every Glob/Grep call in Claude Code — your assistant reads `GRAPH_REPORT.md` and navigates by graph structure instead of keyword-searching every file.
- **`/graphify query`**, **`/graphify path`**, and **`/graphify explain`** let you traverse `graph.json` hop-by-hop from the terminal or inside your assistant.
- The graph **persists across sessions** — ask questions weeks later without re-reading everything.
- Every edge is tagged EXTRACTED, INFERRED, or AMBIGUOUS with a confidence score — honest audit trail of what was found vs inferred.
- Works on code, PDFs, papers, markdown, screenshots, diagrams, and video (Whisper transcription).

If the video only showed the HTML visualization, it missed the core use case. The graph viz is a nice way to explore, but the reason people use it is so their AI assistant understands a codebase's architecture before touching anything.

Thanks for the thorough writeup — this is a documentation clarity issue, not missing functionality.

**The `/graphify` prefix matters.** Commands prefixed with `/` are AI skill commands — you type them in your AI coding assistant (Claude Code, Codex, etc.), not in a terminal shell. The skill file tells your assistant how to interpret them and what Python/CLI calls to make underneath.

So the split is:

| What you type | Where | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| `graphify install` | Terminal | Installs the skill file |
| `graphify query "..."` | Terminal | Directly queries `graph.json` via BFS/DFS |
| `graphify benchmark` | Terminal | Runs benchmark |
| `/graphify .` | AI assistant | AI reads skill, runs full pipeline |
| `/graphify path "A" "B"` | AI assistant | AI traverses `graph.json` hop-by-hop |
| `/graphify explain "X"` | AI assistant | AI looks up node + neighbors |
| `/graphify add <url>` | AI assistant | AI fetches URL, saves to `./raw`, updates graph |
| `/graphify ./raw --update` | AI assistant | AI re-extracts only changed files |
| `/graphify ./raw --watch` | AI assistant | AI starts the watch process |

The README section around line 200 does mix the two syntaxes in a way that reads as if they're all terminal commands — that's worth fixing. We should prefix the skill commands with a comment or header making it clear they belong in your AI assistant, not a shell.

Problem

  The global symbol table added in #[prev-pr] resolves cross-file calls for all languages, but it has a known weakness: name collisions. If two files define a function with the same name (e.g. process, init, run), the global table maps that name to whichever node was
  inserted first. A call in a third file may resolve to the wrong target.

  Proposed fix

  Use import statements to constrain which file a callee can come from, before falling back to the global table.

  Two-step resolution:

  1. Import map pass — before resolving calls, parse each file's import statements and build a per-file map: {imported_name → source_file}. For example:
    - Python: from utils import helper → helper comes from utils.py
    - JS/TS: import { helper } from './utils' → helper comes from utils.ts
    - Go: import "pkg/utils" → utils.Method comes from that package
    - Java: import com.example.Utils → Utils comes from that class file
  2. Constrained lookup — when resolving an unresolved call, first check if the callee name appears in the file's import map. If yes, only match nodes whose source_file matches the imported file. Fall back to the global table only if no import-constrained match exists.

  Impact

  - Eliminates false positives for common function names
  - Makes INFERRED edges nearly as reliable as EXTRACTED ones for well-structured codebases
  - No changes to AST parsing — works by post-processing the existing imports/imports_from edges already in the graph
  -

> > So it handles large repos fine, you just pick a smaller scope. If you want to process everything at once you can split it into a few runs and use --update to merge results incrementally.

**Should you pre-summarize?** No — drop the raw files in as-is. graphify's semantic extraction is specifically designed for long-form content: it runs parallel Claude subagents over chunks of files, extracts named concepts and relationships, and builds a graph from those — not from the full text. /graphify ./newsletters/2020  # first batch
/graphify ./newsletters/2021 --update  # merge into existing graph
/graphify ./newsletters/2022 --update  # keep going
```

Confirming this on a real-world Next.js 16 + TypeScript codebase. `graphify v0.4.11`, AST   
  extraction only (no semantic layer), ~1,072 TS/TSX files. Every import in the project uses
  the `@/*` → `src/*` alias — the Next.js default.                                            
   
  **Impact in numbers:**                                                                      
                                                                       
  | Metric | Value |                                                                          
  |---|---|                                                            
  | Total nodes | 1,794 |
  | Total edges | 1,002 |
  | `imports_from` edges | **0** |
  | Orphan nodes (degree 0) | 558 (**31%**) |                                                 
  | Edge types present | `contains` (893), `calls` (93), `method` (16) |                      
                                                                                              
  Every `import { x } from '@/foo/bar'` is silently dropped, so entire layers of the project  
  end up as disconnected nodes. Next.js App Router route handlers (`src/app/api/**/route.ts`) 
  are the worst-hit because they have no incoming imports either — they're discovered by      
  filesystem routing — so they show up as fully isolated nodes with degree 0, losing all their
   outbound `imports_from` edges on top.

  **Reproduced the root cause in `graphify/extract.py` `_import_js()`** (lines ~142–172):     
   
  ```python

Great use case — graphify can handle it, but 70,000 documents is large so here's what to keep in mind:

**What works well:**
- graphify stores everything in `graph.json` (a networkx node-link format), so queries are graph traversals — fast and token-efficient regardless of corpus size
- The `--update` flag does incremental extraction (only new/changed files), so you don't re-process everything on each run
- Semantic extraction results are cached per file hash, so re-runs are mostly free after the first pass

**Practical limits:**
- The first full extraction will cost API tokens proportional to your doc count — budget accordingly (rough estimate: ~20-25 docs per LLM call)
- `graph.json` for 70k docs will be large (potentially several hundred MB); loading time at MCP server start will be a few seconds
- Consider splitting into domain subgraphs if the documents fall into distinct topic areas — query each subgraph separately for better precision

**Recommended approach for 70k docs:**
1. Organize into subfolders by domain/topic
2. Run `graphify <subfolder>` on each — you get one graph per domain
3. Start the MCP server per domain: `graphify <subfolder> --mcp`

I see that Graphify has predicates in its graph model. As I understand it, those are **system-inferred** (semantic extraction at ingest/query time). Declared and inferred are different primitives:

- **Declared** encodes what the *author* committed to at writing time. Persists through re-indexing, survives model changes, and uses the author's own vocabulary (sovereign per-collection).

2. Layer inferred predicates on top as enrichment, with **provenance preserved on each edge** (author-asserted vs. system-inferred)

This is a real issue. The skill prompt tells the LLM to use `filename:symbol` as node IDs, but the AST extractor generates IDs like `module.symbol` (dot-separated, no file extension). When the LLM invents IDs that do not match what the extractor produces, edges between semantic and code nodes point to non-existent targets.

The cleanest fix is a deterministic ID rule in both the skill prompt and the extractor: strip the extension from the filename, replace path separators with dots, and append the symbol name. Example: `src/auth/session.py` + `validate_token` becomes `auth.session.validate_token`. That way the LLM can reconstruct the exact ID from context without guessing.

Those relation types were chosen to cover the full spectrum of edges that appear across code, documentation, and research paper corpora without collapsing semantically distinct relationships into a single generic "related" edge.

- **calls / implements / references** -- structural code relationships derivable from AST (call sites, interface implementations, import/use statements)
- **cites** -- bibliography links in papers and docs
- **conceptually_related_to** -- soft semantic affinity when no harder edge fits (two modules that share domain vocabulary but have no direct code link)
- **shares_data_with** -- data-flow hint: two nodes read or write the same schema, table, or struct field
- **semantically_similar_to** -- near-duplicate detection (two functions that do the same thing under different names)
- **rationale_for** -- a design decision node that explains why another node exists (common in ADRs and comment blocks)

The set is intentionally broader than a pure call graph so that the LLM can express nuance when it finds it. If you are working on a code-only corpus and only care about structural edges, the `calls`, `implements`, and `references` types are the ones that matter most.

Good summary of the pain points. Here is the intended workflow and answers to each question.

**Intended workflow: single source of truth, not multi-contributor regeneration.**

The graph is a build artifact, not source. Treat it like a compiled binary: one person (or CI) regenerates it, everyone else consumes it.

1. **LLM non-determinism** -- this is by design. Running `/graphify .` twice on the same files will produce slightly different graphs because the LLM is non-deterministic. The fix is to designate one maintainer or a CI job as the sole graph publisher. Other contributors run `/graphify --query` against the committed graph; they do not regenerate it.

2. **manifest.json mtime drift** -- you are right that git does not preserve mtimes, so `--update` will re-process everything after a fresh clone. The mitigation is to gitignore `manifest.json` and treat it as local state. The cache (once committed) does the real deduplication -- if the file content hash matches, extraction is skipped regardless of mtime.

3. **Cache sharing** -- yes, committing `cache/` is safe now that keys are content-addressed (#311). It trades repo size for speed: contributors skip re-extraction for files that have not changed. Whether the tradeoff is worth it depends on how large your corpus is.

**Recommended CI setup:**
- Run `/graphify .` (or `graphify --update`) in CI on every merge to main
- Commit `graph.json`, `graph.html`, `GRAPH_REPORT.md`, and optionally `cache/`
- Gitignore `manifest.json`
- Contributors query the committed graph; they do not regenerate it locally unless they are the designated graph maintainer

Happy to add a "Team workflow" section to the docs if you want to draft one.

This is an accurate description of the current limitation. The cross-file call resolution in `_resolve_cross_file_imports()` is Python-only and import-level only -- it does not trace actual call sites, and all other languages have zero cross-file resolution from AST.

The reason it works this way is that full cross-file call resolution requires building a per-language scope/symbol table across the entire corpus before emitting any edges, which is a significant amount of work to get right for each language. The current implementation trades completeness for speed and simplicity.

The semantic subagents compensate for this on mixed corpora -- the LLM can reason across files and emit cross-file edges that AST misses. For code-only corpora (no LLM), the gap is real.

A proper fix would require:
1. A two-pass extraction: first pass builds a corpus-wide symbol table (exported symbols per file), second pass resolves call sites against it.
2. Per-language import resolution (each language has different import semantics).

This is on the roadmap but there is no timeline. For now, the LLM semantic pass is the intended mechanism for cross-file relationship discovery on mixed corpora.

Tested this PR end-to-end on a real TypeScript codebase (~1,400 TS/TSX files, 22 aliases in `compilerOptions.paths`). Found a silent failure that prevents the patch from taking effect in most real projects:

**`tsconfig.json` is JSONC by default**, not strict JSON. TypeScript's own spec allows line/block comments and trailing commas, and virtually every tsconfig generated by `tsc --init`, Next.js, Vite, React Native, etc. ships with `/* ... */` annotations on every option.

`json.loads(tsconfig_path.read_text(...))` raises `JSONDecodeError`, the except clause returns `{}`, aliases are never loaded, and the rest of the PR is a no-op. No error surfaces to the user.

Measured impact on a real corpus (after fixing locally):

```
imports_ratio:    3.0% → 23.8%   (10.3x, +4,786 edges)
isolated nodes:   361 → 53       (-85%)
communities:      531 → 133      (-75%, fragmentation collapsed)
```

The naive regex strip (`/\*.*?\*/`) breaks on string literals like `"@assets/*"` — the `/*` inside the string gets consumed. A string-aware pass handles it correctly:

```python
raw = tsconfig_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
out: list[str] = []
i, n = 0, len(raw)
while i < n:
    c = raw[i]
    if c == '"':
        j = i + 1
        while j < n:
            if raw[j] == "\\" and j + 1 < n:
                j += 2
                continue
            if raw[j] == '"':
                j += 1
                break
            j += 1
        out.append(raw[i:j])
        i = j
    elif c == "/" and i + 1 < n and raw[i + 1] == "/":
        nl = raw.find("\n", i)
        i = n if nl == -1 else nl
    elif c == "/" and i + 1 < n and raw[i + 1] == "*":
        end = raw.find("*/", i + 2)
        i = n if end == -1 else end + 2
    else:
        out.append(c)
        i += 1
stripped = re.sub(r",\s*([}\]])", r"\1", "".join(out))
data = json.loads(stripped)
```

Handles: `//` line comments, `/* */` block comments (including multi-line), trailing commas, and string literals containing `/*`, `//` or `"` (with escape handling).

### What I can contribute

**Conversation ingestion** — I already have working parsers for both Claude Code JSONL and Desktop export formats. They output markdown with YAML frontmatter (date, project, topics, files_touched). Happy to clean them up and submit a PR as a starting point for native implementation.

One thing we learned the hard way: Claude Code JSONL messages nest content inside `msg.message.content`, not `msg.content` directly. And `content` can be a string (user messages) or a list of blocks with `type: text/tool_use/thinking` (assistant messages). The first version of our parser returned empty files because it looked in the wrong place.

### Lessons from building this

Some things we discovered during development that might inform v5.0:

**1. GRAPH_REPORT.md size matters more than you'd think.** We initially ran graphify on a 1,777-file workspace. The report was 145KB / 2,742 lines. Loading this in context defeated the purpose — the agent spent tokens reading the report instead of reading raw files. We ended up needing a separate "brain summary" at ~3KB. A `--summary` or `--compact` flag would solve this natively.

**2. AST god nodes are noisy at scale.** On a mixed-language workspace, the top god nodes were `GET()`, `error()`, `info()`, `close()` — generic method names connecting everything. The semantic nodes (actual project concepts) were buried. For multi-project setups, a semantic-only graph mode (skip AST, just extract concepts from docs) was far more useful as a navigation aid.

**3. Per-project beats monolithic.** Running graphify on the entire workspace produced 384 communities, most of them single-node isolates from old Desktop chat topics. Running on individual projects produced 19 focused communities with meaningful structure. The multi-project mode should probably generate per-project graphs with a lightweight cross-project index on top, not one massive graph.

**4. The PreToolUse hook needs a global fallback path.** If the user works from their home directory (not the project root), `graphify-out/GRAPH_REPORT.md` doesn't exist relative to cwd. The hook silently does nothing. A configurable search path (check cwd, then check known project directories) would help.

**5. Lightweight extraction without LLM.** For 366 Desktop conversations, we used keyword matching + YAML frontmatter parsing instead of subagent extraction — 366 nodes, 125 edges, zero tokens. For conversation files specifically, this regex/NLP approach might be better than full semantic extraction.

**6. Windows `graphify claude install` fails on Cyrillic paths.** `UnicodeEncodeError: 'charmap' codec can't encode characters` when the working directory contains non-ASCII characters (common on non-English Windows). We had to install the hook manually.

### Priority suggestion

Compact report mode would be the quickest win for multi-project adoption. Right now, the choice is between "load the full report (expensive)" and "don't load it (agent is blind)." A 2-3KB summary per project would make the hierarchy pattern work out of the box.

Conversation ingestion would be second — it's the missing piece that connects "what we built" with "what we discussed about it."

@ctf0 `pipx` is basically a wrapper for pip and virtualenv, so packages are isolated from one another into separate environments. This means you need to install `watchdog` to the same virtual environment as graphify, and to do that you can use the extras syntax, i.e. the brackets suffix. 

As per the `pyproject.toml`:

https://github.com/safishamsi/graphify/blob/7a0a5ac1fb71b02b13fe0cd329971a29ea960b28/pyproject.toml#L48

you simply run

```bash
pipx install 'graphifyy[watch]'
```

You can also specify multiple extras at once, e.g.

```bash
# watchdog, pypdf, and html2text
pipx install 'graphifyy[watch,pdf]'

# all optional dependencies
pipx install 'graphifyy[all]'
```

However, that will not work if you already have graphify installed, so you'll need to either reinstall the entire graphifyy package by adding the `--force` flag,

```bash
pipx install --force 'graphifyy[watch]'
```

or by injecting the dependency into your existing graphifyy environment:

```bash
pipx inject graphifyy 'graphifyy[watch]'
```

the `inject` command is also useful for e.g. adding packages that aren't defined in `pyproject.toml`,

```bash
pipx inject graphifyy pycowsay
```

> Good summary of the pain points. Here is the intended workflow and answers to each question.
> 
> **Intended workflow: single source of truth, not multi-contributor regeneration.**
> 
> The graph is a build artifact, not source. Treat it like a compiled binary: one person (or CI) regenerates it, everyone else consumes it.
> 
> 1. **LLM non-determinism** -- this is by design. Running `/graphify .` twice on the same files will produce slightly different graphs because the LLM is non-deterministic. The fix is to designate one maintainer or a CI job as the sole graph publisher. Other contributors run `/graphify --query` against the committed graph; they do not regenerate it.
> 2. **manifest.json mtime drift** -- you are right that git does not preserve mtimes, so `--update` will re-process everything after a fresh clone. The mitigation is to gitignore `manifest.json` and treat it as local state. The cache (once committed) does the real deduplication -- if the file content hash matches, extraction is skipped regardless of mtime.
> 3. **Cache sharing** -- yes, committing `cache/` is safe now that keys are content-addressed ([Cache uses absolute paths in hash, making it non-portable across machines #311](https://github.com/safishamsi/graphify/issues/311)). It trades repo size for speed: contributors skip re-extraction for files that have not changed. Whether the tradeoff is worth it depends on how large your corpus is.
> 
> **Recommended CI setup:**
> 
> * Run `/graphify .` (or `graphify --update`) in CI on every merge to main
> * Commit `graph.json`, `graph.html`, `GRAPH_REPORT.md`, and optionally `cache/`
> * Gitignore `manifest.json`
> * Contributors query the committed graph; they do not regenerate it locally unless they are the designated graph maintainer
> 
> Happy to add a "Team workflow" section to the docs if you want to draft one.

**Severity:** action required | **Category:** correctness

**How to fix:** Don’t clear flag in code rebuild

**Agent prompt to fix** - you can give this to your LLM of choice:

> ### Issue description
> `graphify-out/needs_update` is written for non-code changes requiring semantic re-extraction (`/graphify --update`), but the new `check_update()` path triggers `_rebuild_code()` (AST-only) and that function clears the same flag. This can leave the graph stale while removing the only signal that an update is required.
> 
> ### Issue Context
> - `_notify_only()` writes the flag for non-code changes.
> - `check_update()` uses the presence of that flag as its trigger.
> - `_rebuild_code()` performs code-only rebuild and unlinks the flag.
> 
> ### Fix Focus Areas
> - graphify/watch.py[21-76]
> - graphify/watch.py[87-107]
> 
> ### Suggested fix
> Either:
> 1) Stop clearing `needs_update` inside `_rebuild_code()`; only clear it after the appropriate semantic update pipeline completes, OR
> 2) Use separate flags (e.g., `needs_code_rebuild` vs `needs_semantic_update`) and have `check_update` handle only the code-rebuild flag.

I'm not familiar with the codebase, so I asked a generic Copilot agent to review it:
Findings (ordered by severity):

Critical: cross-file edge targets can remain stale after renaming In the rename pass, edge remapping is keyed only by the edge source_file, then applied to both source and target IDs ([extract.py:3225]. But cross-file uses edges are created with source_file set to the importing file while target points to a node in another file ([extract.py:2651]. Result: when a target node from file B is renamed, an edge originating in file A may not update its target, leaving dangling/mismatched IDs. High: unresolved-call edges may reference old caller IDs Raw calls store caller_nid before the collision-disambiguation step ([extract.py:1071], [extract.py:1072]. Colliding nodes are later renamed ([extract.py:3203]. During cross-file raw call resolution, the caller is read directly from raw_calls with no remap ([extract.py:3258], [extract.py:3262]). Result: inferred calls can be emitted from non-existent source IDs after rename. High: replacement ID can still collide and silently drop nodes New IDs are built from only the parent directory name + old ID ([extract.py:3200], [extract.py:3201]. If two colliding files have the same parent directory name in different paths (for example, src/app/Program.cs and tests/app/Program.cs), both compute the same replacement ID, and one is dropped by seen_final_ids ([extract.py:3202], [extract.py:3206]. This reintroduces merge/loss behavior in a common monorepo layout.

The main issue is that this does not take into account the full path after the current working directory when generating the ID. It would also be useful to add unit tests to cover these cases.

**Root cause confirmed:** `_rebuild_code()` was clearing `needs_update`, but that flag is written exclusively by `_notify_only()` for non-code changes (docs, images, papers) that require LLM-backed semantic re-extraction. I’d sequence it like this:

1. lead distribution with the coding-assistant / codebase-understanding wedge
2. keep the broader knowledge-graph story as the platform expansion behind it

Reason: the broader knowledge-graph vision is probably more defensible long-term, but it is also harder to explain in one breath and harder to spread repo-native. The coding wedge is easier for GitHub, easier for word of mouth, and easier for someone to try immediately.

So to answer the traction split directly: if the goal is repo growth, I’d optimize the top-level README and first demo for the dev use case first. Then, once that wedge is winning consistently, expand the narrative into the larger personal/work knowledge graph story on the site, docs, and roadmap.

Put differently: use coding-assistant distribution to earn attention, then cash that attention into the broader category.

The current README is already moving in the right direction because it opens with the assistant use case while still preserving the bigger ambition underneath. I’d keep pushing that sequencing rather than trying to make both stories carry equal weight at the top.

Hi @safishamsi — verified v0.4.32 on Windows 11 / PowerShell 7.6.1. The
*.exe case works for explicit .exe paths, but the warning still fires for *pip
Windows shims without extension*.
Repro

$ command -v graphify
/c/Users/matteo.truppa/AppData/Local/Programs/Python/Python312/Scripts/graphify

$ ls -la $(command -v graphify)
-rwxr-xr-x 1 user 1049089 108373 Apr 23 15:36 /c/Users/.../Scripts/graphify

It's a 108KB binary shim (pip console_scripts entry point on Windows) named
graphify *without* .exe. The case statement falls through to *) → head -1
on the binary → warning returns on line 23.
Commit output (graphifyy 0.4.32, hook reinstalled via hook uninstall &&
hook install)

$ git commit --allow-empty -m "test"
.git/hooks/post-commit: line 23: warning: command substitution:
ignored null byte in input
[graphify watch] Rebuilt: 16 nodes, 13 edges, 5 communities

Functional fallback still works (python3 takes over), warning remains
cosmetic but visible.
Proposed fix — probe shebang magic bytes

case "$GRAPHIFY_BIN" in
    *.exe) _SHEBANG="" ;;
    *)
        # Probe: is it a text shebang script or a binary shim?
        if head -c 2 "$GRAPHIFY_BIN" 2>/dev/null | grep -q '^#!'; then
            _SHEBANG=$(head -1 "$GRAPHIFY_BIN" | sed 's/^#![[:space:]]*//')
        else
            _SHEBANG=""
        fi
        ;;
esac

Covers: pip Windows shim (no extension), Linux/macOS text scripts, future
binary wrappers on any OS. Zero functional change where current logic
already works (text shebangs still read normally).

Hi, extract() returns cached JS/TS extraction results keyed only by the source file hash, but extract_js() now depends on tsconfig.json (paths/baseUrl). Changing tsconfig.json will not invalidate cached results, so import edges can remain wrong until the source files change or the cache is cleared.

**Severity:** action required | **Category:** correctness

**How to fix:** Include tsconfig in cache key

**Agent prompt to fix** - you can give this to your LLM of choice:

> ## Issue description
> JS/TS extraction is now tsconfig-dependent (paths/baseUrl), but the extraction cache is keyed only by the source file contents. This causes stale `imports_from` edges when `tsconfig.json` changes.
> 
> ## Issue Context
> - `extract()` uses `load_cached()` and skips calling `extract_js()` when a cache entry exists.
> - `load_cached()` is keyed by `file_hash(path)` which hashes only the code file contents + resolved path.
> - `extract_js()` calls `load_tsconfig_paths(path.parent)` and changes edge targets based on tsconfig.
> 
> ## Fix Focus Areas
> - graphify/extract.py[1103-1119]
> - graphify/extract.py[2653-2660]
> - graphify/cache.py[10-17]
> - graphify/cache.py[27-44]
> 
> ## Suggested approach
> - Make the per-file cache key include the effective tsconfig.json used for that file (e.g., hash/mtime of the found tsconfig.json + baseUrl/paths content), or
> - Store alias-map-related metadata in the cached result and validate it on load (recompute if tsconfig changed), or
> - Disable cache reuse for JS/TS when a tsconfig.json is present unless the cache is scoped to the tsconfig content.

Hi, `save_cached()` creates a raw file descriptor via `tempfile.mkstemp()` and then wraps it with `os.fdopen()`, but if `os.fdopen()` raises before owning the fd, the descriptor is leaked and the temp file may become undeletable (notably on Windows). This is a production-path resource leak that can accumulate in long-running runs or leave orphan `.tmp` files.

**Severity:** action required | **Category:** reliability

**How to fix:** Ensure fd closed on failure

**Agent prompt to fix** - you can give this to your LLM of choice:

> ### Issue description
> `graphify/cache.py::save_cached` uses `tempfile.mkstemp()` + `os.fdopen()`. If `os.fdopen()` raises before taking ownership of the fd, the fd leaks and the temp file may be left behind / undeletable.
> 
> ### Issue Context
> `mkstemp()` returns an already-open OS fd. It must be closed even when `fdopen()` fails.
> 
> ### Fix Focus Areas
> - graphify/cache.py[102-123]
> 
> ### Suggested fix
> Refactor to a pattern that guarantees closure:
> - Option A (preferred): use `tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(mode="w", encoding="utf-8", dir=..., prefix=..., suffix=..., delete=False)` and write via the file object; capture `tmp = Path(f.name)`; close occurs via the context manager.
> - Option B: wrap `os.fdopen(fd, ...)` in an inner try/except and `os.close(fd)` if `fdopen` fails, then re-raise.
> 
> Keep the existing cleanup logic (`tmp.unlink(missing_ok=True)` on exceptions) and the atomic `os.replace` behavior.

+1, hitting this on a TypeScript pnpm monorepo (~2,400 files, 5,047 nodes after AST extraction). Adding a complementary data point because the multi-copy-helper pattern below isn't covered by the existing report or by the v0.5.5 #598 fix.

## Setup

- graphifyy v0.5.5 (post #598)
- Corpus: 2,408 `.ts/.tsx` files (after filtering out `e2e/`, tests, stories, mocks, `.d.ts`, configs)
- Pure AST run (`document=image=paper=0` → semantic Part B skipped)

## Reproducer pattern: same-named helper duplicated across sibling apps

The monorepo has the same helper *re-implemented* per app — not just a common short name in one file:

```
apps/train/shared/src/helpers/project/getPhaseHelper.ts        :: getPhaseFromHost()
apps/airport/end-airport/shared/helpers/url/getPhase.ts        :: getPhaseFromHost()
apps/subway/cs-subwayline/src/helpers/project/getPhaseFromHost.ts :: getPhaseFromHost()
```

`extract.py` (v0.5.5 L3181–L3210) builds `global_label_to_nid` with **last-write-wins** dict semantics on the lowercased label, so all three definitions collapse to whichever file the loop visited last. In my run that was the subway one. Result:

| `getPhaseFromHost` definition | location | degree | `EXTRACTED` | `INFERRED` |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| subway/cs-subwayline | (winner) | **89** | 1 | **88** |
| train/shared | (loser) | 3 | 3 | 0 |
| airport/end-airport | (loser) | 1 | 1 | 0 |

The 88 INFERRED edges land on the **wrong** definition. Callers in `apps/train/end/`, `apps/ferry/src/`, `apps/airport/end-airport/` etc. are reported as calling subway's helper — they aren't.

This is the same root pattern as the report's `log()` / `execute()` / `optional()`, but worth flagging separately: in a monorepo it isn't a "common short name" issue — it's structurally guaranteed to happen for **any helper duplicated across workspace packages**, even when the name is uniquely descriptive (`getPhaseFromHost`, `sendClickLog`, `getApiBasePath`, `getEncryptUrl`).

## Side note: v0.5.5's #598 fix doesn't cover this

The `is_member_call` skip in #598 helped one related class (e.g. `t()` from `const { t } = useTranslation()` is no longer a 106-degree phantom in my graph — confirmed dropped to degree 1–2 with `EXTRACTED` only after upgrade). But the bare-call resolution path is unchanged, so multi-copy helpers stay broken.

Before/after on the top phantoms in this corpus:

| god node | v0.4.23 deg (INFERRED) | v0.5.5 deg (INFERRED) | status |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `t()` | 106 (105) | 1 (0) | ✅ fixed |
| `Map()` | 95 (90) | gone | ✅ fixed |
| `filter()` | 56 (?) | gone | ✅ fixed |
| `Home()` | 35 (?) | gone | ✅ fixed |
| `requestGet()` | 103 (102) | **109 (108)** | ❌ unchanged — single shared definition, may be largely *correct* but indistinguishable from phantom |
| `getPhaseFromHost()` | 85 (84) | **89 (88)** | ❌ unchanged, multi-copy phantom |
| `getApiBasePath()` | 75 (72) | 78 (75) | ❌ unchanged |
| `sendClickLog()` | 66 (63) | 67 (64) | ❌ unchanged |

So v0.5.5 cleanly cleared the destructure / `new X()` / JSX class of phantoms but left the helper-duplication class in place — and #543 is still the right home for it.

## Re: proposed fixes

For monorepos specifically, **(b) gate on actual import statements** is the only proposal that distinguishes legitimate `requestGet` calls (single shared definition genuinely imported by 100+ callers) from misattributed `getPhaseFromHost` calls (3 definitions, callers should resolve to whichever their file imports). Cardinality alone can't disambiguate these.

A weaker but cheap heuristic if (b) is too invasive: when `len(candidates_for_label) > 1`, prefer the candidate whose `source_file` shares the longest directory prefix with the caller's `source_file`. That alone would route `apps/train/end/...` callers to `apps/train/shared/.../getPhaseHelper.ts` instead of subway. Confidence stays `INFERRED` either way, but the *target* becomes correct.

(c) "trusted degree" postprocessing helps the audit signal but doesn't fix the merged-into-wrong-target problem when other tools downstream consume `graph.json`.

In `graphifyy 0.5.4`, `extract.py` builds the cross-file resolver map as a single-value dict:

```py
# extract.py:3401-3406
global_label_to_nid: dict[str, str] = {}
for n in all_nodes:
    raw = n.get("label", "")
    normalised = raw.strip("()").lstrip(".")

Then unresolved calls use only that last-written target:

```py

tgt = global_label_to_nid.get(callee.lower())

"confidence_score": 0.8,
```

So even after the v0.5.5 member-call fix from #598, duplicate bare helpers still have a separate failure mode: `foo()` defined in multiple sibling packages collapses to whichever node was visited last, and every unresolved `foo` call points there. This is not just over-linking; it can actively route the edge to the wrong definition.

Suggested shape of the fix: change the resolver map to `label -> list[candidate]`; if there is exactly one candidate, current behavior can remain. Thanks for the quick response and for adding the additional VCS markers and the home directory guard! That prevents the most extreme "drive-root" leakage.

However, I’d like to request that we reopen this to consider a more "hermetic" discovery strategy. While the home directory guard is a great safety net, it doesn't solve the Project-to-Project leakage problem.

### The Remaining Failure Mode

Imagine a developer's workspace structure:
```
/work/
  ├── .graphifyignore  (generic rules for work)
  ├── project-alpha/   (No VCS, standalone)
  └── project-beta/    (No VCS, standalone)
```

If I run ```graphify .``` inside project-alpha, the current logic will still climb to ```/work/``` and apply those ignore rules. This is counter-intuitive; as a user, when I point a tool at a specific folder, I expect that folder to be the "Source of Truth" unless the folder is explicitly part of a larger, recognized Unit (like a Git repository).

  }
}

- `graphifyy 0.6.5`

In `graphify/__main__.py`, change the `hook-check` command so it exits successfully without printing unsupported `hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext`.

    graph = Path("graphify-out") / "graph.json"
    if graph.exists():
        import json as _json

You're reading the code right, and your three answers in order are: **no, yes, and not officially - but it's a 50-line wrapper away.**

**1. Is there a headless CLI for semantic LLM extraction?**

No. `graphify update <path>` calls `graphify.extract.extract`, which dispatches on file extension via `_DISPATCH`. That dict only contains code extensions — no `.md`, `.rst`, `.txt`. For a docs-only corpus every file falls through returning `{"nodes": [], "edges": []}`. So `update` legitimately produces nothing for you.

The CLI (`__main__.py`) exposes `install`, `update`, `query`, `path`, `explain`, `export`, and a few others. **There is no `extract`/`ingest` subcommand that calls an LLM.**

**2. Is the intended model "human runs `/graphify --update` after each merge"?**

Today, yes. The `/graphify` skill is the only orchestrator that knows how to chunk docs, dispatch Claude Code subagents, merge results, run clustering, and generate reports. It runs interactively inside Claude Code.

**3. Is headless semantic extraction on the roadmap?**

Most of it is **already implemented as a library, just not wired to the CLI.** `graphify/llm.py` exposes `extract_corpus_parallel(files, backend='kimi'|'claude', ...)` with token-budget chunking, parallel execution, and adaptive retry. The skill itself uses it: if `MOONSHOT_API_KEY` is set, it calls `extract_corpus_parallel` directly instead of dispatching Claude subagents — so the headless path exists, just behind the skill boundary.

**Workaround today** — call the library directly in CI:

```bash
pip install 'graphifyy[kimi]'   # or [claude]
export MOONSHOT_API_KEY=...     # or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
```

```python
from pathlib import Path
from graphify.detect import detect
from graphify.llm import extract_corpus_parallel
from graphify.build import build_from_json
from graphify.cluster import cluster
from graphify.export import to_json

root = Path('docs')
files = [Path(f) for f in detect(root)['files']['document']]
result = extract_corpus_parallel(files, backend='kimi', root=root)
G = build_from_json(result)
to_json(G, cluster(G), 'graphify-out/graph.json', force=True)
```

This gives you a real semantic graph from a docs-only corpus in CI today, no Claude Code in the loop.

**What a first-class `graphify extract` subcommand would look like:** wire the above into `__main__.py` — the library work is done, it's a ~50-line CLI entry point. The one thing you'd lose vs the interactive skill is LLM-generated community labels (the skill picks names in an interactive pass). That's presentational; your `graph.json` and `GRAPH_REPORT.md` would be complete. A headless `graphify extract` subcommand is a reasonable addition — happy to take a PR or track it as a feature request.

Update: we've shipped a fix in the next commit.

`graphify extract` is now a first-class CLI subcommand:

```bash
pip install --upgrade graphifyy

# docs-only corpus in CI:
export MOONSHOT_API_KEY=...   # or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
graphify extract ./docs
```

Flags:
- `--backend kimi|claude` — explicit backend (auto-detected from env if omitted)
- `--out DIR` — output root (default: same as `<path>`, writes `<path>/graphify-out/`)
- `--no-cluster` — skip community detection, write raw extraction only

**What it does:** detect → AST extract on code files → semantic LLM extract on docs/papers/images → merge → build → cluster → write `graph.json` + `.graphify_analysis.json`.

Your docs-only case works cleanly: if there are no code files, the AST step is skipped and only the LLM extraction runs. Prints token counts and estimated cost after each run.

Hit a related-but-distinct case of the same bug class on a 1,873-file SvelteKit codebase, supporting this PR's design. Worth flagging here in case it shapes the implementation.

This PR's evidence covers same-pair *multi-relation* collapse (`imports + references`, `method + instantiates`). I additionally observed same-pair *bidirectional-direction* collapse:

- `BlurHash.svelte` imports `compute_scale` from `ImageV2.svelte`
- `ImageV2.svelte` imports `<BlurHash>` from `BlurHash.svelte`

Two real edges in the source. After `build_from_json(result)` in `_rebuild_code` (no `directed=True`), they collapse to a single undirected edge with one direction's information lost. Querying "incoming edges to BlurHash" returns zero, so dead-component / "where is X used" tooling false-flags it.

On this repo: 43 such edges (41 `imports_from`, 2 `calls`) compared to ~13k total — small in absolute terms, but it specifically breaks the bidirectional-import case which is structurally legal and not rare in component libraries.

`MultiDiGraph` (the directed variant of this PR's option) would preserve both ends. So the fix here covers our case too — provided `_rebuild_code` adopts `multigraph=True, directed=True` (or equivalent) once the option lands. Otherwise the option exists but the default code path still drops edges.

Methodology note for anyone validating: `_rebuild_code` preserves nodes/edges from a previous `graph.json` whose IDs aren't in the new AST output, which inflates incremental-rebuild edge counts. Wipe `graphify-out/` fully before measuring impact — I burned a few hours trusting incremental numbers before catching this.

Hit collision-driven node confusion on a 1,873-file SvelteKit codebase that this PR would address. Adding our cases for evidence.

Symptom on our side: 33 self-loops in the graph after extraction. Sampling them, several patterns trace back to `_make_id(stem, name)` collisions where `stem` is too shallow:

- `LinkDomain` (Sequelize model) has a `[shares_data_with]` self-loop because the file node and the class node end up with the same `_make_id` after `_file_stem` truncates to one parent. The model file is `src/lib/server/models/LinkDomain.model.ts` (file_stem `models.LinkDomain.model`), and the exported class is `LinkDomain`. The class's `_make_id(stem, name)` and the file's `_make_id(str(path))` collide at the canonical-ID layer.

- `Comment` model exhibits the same pattern — `models.Comment.model` stem, `Comment` class. Self-loop emitted.

- Multiple `[calls]` self-loops on canonical-rule files that share a parent dir name with sibling files of the same stem.

Repo-wide: ~30 of 33 self-loops are likely this bug class (3 are valid SQL FK self-references on `tags`, `publishers`, `work_collections`).

This PR's deepening strategy (auto-walk to 2+ parents on collision) would resolve all of them. The deepening is a strict superset of fixes — once stems are unique, the canonical-ID collisions go away and the spurious self-loops with them.

One observation worth pinning down: the `models/*.model.ts` pattern is interesting because the file already encodes its kind in the basename (`*.model.ts`). For Sequelize/TypeORM/Mongoose codebases this pattern is dense — dozens of `<Name>.model.ts` files with classes named `<Name>` inside. Even the deepened stem (`models.LinkDomain.model`) collides with the class id (`LinkDomain` qualified to the same stem) at `_make_id`. May be worth verifying the deepening alone resolves it, vs. needing the file-vs-class id namespacing change too.

(Same methodology note as #709 — wipe `graphify-out/` fully before measuring; incremental rebuilds preserve stale data.)

[graphify] single-file chunk docs/README.md truncated at max_completion_tokens — partial result kept
```

A single-file truncation means the file's own extracted JSON exceeds 8192 tokens. Bumping to 16K probably saves this case. But it implies that **for at least some files in dense corpora, no fixed `max_tokens` is safe** — there will always be a file dense enough to push beyond whatever ceiling is set. We can't keep raising the cap forever; output tokens cost real money and add latency, and at some point you bump into the model's hard ceiling (64K for Sonnet 4.6, 128K for 3.7).

The deeper issue, I think, is in how `_pack_chunks_by_tokens` sizes work:

1. It packs by **input** tokens (default 60K). That implicitly assumes a roughly 10:1 input:output ratio — fine for sparse content, broken for dense entity-spec / PRD content where the LLM emits dozens of nodes + edges per file.
2. The adaptive retry treats truncation as a per-call accident and reacts after the fact, paying for the truncated call (full input + 8K wasted output) before splitting. For a corpus where most chunks truncate at depth 0, this overhead compounds.

A few directions that would address the root rather than the cap:

- **Pack by an estimated output budget**, not input budget. E.g., heuristic based on file character count + structural density (count of headers, tables, code blocks). Calibrate from observed output:input ratios in cache.
- **Pre-split files** whose estimated output exceeds the output budget. For Markdown, splitting by `##` sections is usually safe. The cache key would need to include the section identifier, but that's mostly clean.
- **Adapt proactively in-run**: if the first chunk in a run truncates, halve the chunk size for all remaining chunks instead of just splitting that one. One bad chunk usually predicts more.
- **Stream + parse incrementally**: when a stream ends mid-string, salvage everything up to the last complete `{...}` instead of throwing the whole response away. This recovers the wasted output tokens.

For our corpus (1,000+ dense Markdown files), the v0.7.6 16K cap will absorb most cases but I expect we'll still see depth 3 failures on the 5–10% densest files. We'll keep an eye on it after upgrading and report back. Just wanted to flag this so the long-term direction is clear — happy to provide more data or test patches.

Either way, thanks again for the responsive fix.

## Reproduction on a 39-file corpus

**Corpus:** Codex monorepo root (31 Python code files + 8 markdown/yaml docs, ~13k words). Standard `/graphify` invocation, two parallel Claude subagents handled semantic extraction.

After merge, every Python test function existed **twice** in the graph because the two passes label and locate identically-named entities differently:

| Pass | label | source_file root | source_location |
|---|---|---|---|
| AST | `test_settings_users_crud` | `e2e/tests/...` (project-rooted) | `None` |
| Semantic | `test_settings_users_crud()` | `tests/...` (relative) | `L69` |

The skill prompt says *"IDs must be deterministic from the label alone"* — but neither the AST nor the semantic side normalizes the label before hashing, so:

- AST id = `test_org_admin_settings_users_crud`
- Semantic id = `tests_test_org_admin_test_settings_users_crud`

Both pointing at line 69 of the same file. **84 such paren-twin pairs in this single 39-file corpus.**

Knock-on effect: every `--calls-->` edge from `navigate_to_tab()` exists twice (once EXTRACTED to the AST node, once INFERRED to its phantom twin). `navigate_to_tab()` reported degree 31 — 16 real edges plus 15 duplicate phantoms.

## Post-processing fix that works (no LLM tokens)

Two passes on `graph.json`:

```python
def norm(label): return re.sub(r'\(\s*\)$', '', (label or '')).strip().lower()
def basename(p):  return (p or '').rsplit('/', 1)[-1]

# Group by (normalized_label, basename(source_file)) only — ignore source_location
# because AST often has it as None while semantic provides it.
groups = defaultdict(list)
for nid, n in nodes.items():
    key = (norm(n['label']), basename(n.get('source_file','')))
    if key[0] and key[1]:
        groups[key].append(nid)

# Canonical = label without trailing "()", then shortest id (AST nodes win)
remap = {}
for key, ids in groups.items():
    if len(ids) < 2: continue
    canonical = min(ids, key=lambda i: (1 if nodes[i]['label'].endswith('()') else 0, len(i)))
    for nid in ids:
        if nid != canonical:
            # Graft non-null source_location from absorbed twin onto canonical
            if not nodes[canonical].get('source_location') and nodes[nid].get('source_location'):
                nodes[canonical]['source_location'] = nodes[nid]['source_location']
            remap[nid] = canonical

# Apply remap to edges + hyperedges, drop self-loops, dedupe by (s, t, relation)
# Then `graphify cluster-only` to refresh communities.
```

## Result

| Metric | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| Nodes | 373 | **154** |
| Edges | 392 | **212** |
| Communities | 51 | **13** |
| Weakly-connected (deg ≤ 1) | 195 (52%) | **52 (34%)** |
| Singleton communities | 23 | 2 |
| `navigate_to_tab()` degree | 31 (15 phantom) | **16 (real)** |
| Procurement E2E cohesion | (split across stubs) | **0.39** |
| Project Detail cohesion | (split across stubs) | **0.36** |

Communities went from "mostly named after a single function" to clean topical clusters: *Page Object Helpers & Auth Fixtures*, *Codex Submodule Architecture*, *Persona Fixtures & Playwright Doc*, *Login Flow E2E*, *Docker Compose Stack*, etc. The Playwright-doc → fixtures → helpers cross-cluster bridge survived the cleanup intact, which suggests the remap is preserving real signal.

In `merge_ast_semantic` (or wherever the two extractions are unioned), apply the `(norm_label, basename)` canonicalization before inserting semantic nodes into the existing AST graph. The label pairing is robust because the semantic agent reliably emits `function_name()` labels and the AST extractor emits `function_name`. If a project diverges from that convention, falling back to `(norm_label, basename, source_location)` when `source_location` is non-null on both sides catches the rest.

**Addendum: UX, Observability & Hard Timeouts during Local Inference**

Further testing on a large corpus (383 docs) has revealed a critical issue regarding connection stability with local backends:

1. **The "Hard" HTTP Timeout:** Even with a high-end GPU (RTX 5090), processing a 16k token chunk with a 31B model can take longer than the default 60-second timeout of the `openai` Python client. Since `llm.py` does not specify a custom timeout during client initialization, the process aborts prematurely: `[graphify] chunk 3/26 failed: Request timed out.`
2. **Lack of Progress Telemetry:** There is currently no live progress bar (e.g., via `tqdm`) for semantic extraction. Users cannot see if a chunk is being processed or if the system is truly hung.

**Proposed Technical Fixes:**

* **Configurable Timeout:** Expose an `api_timeout` parameter (defaulting to 600s or None for local backends) in the configuration.
* **Progress Bar:** Implement a progress bar in `extract_corpus_parallel` to track chunk completion.
* **Persistent Logs:** Write an execution log to `/graphify-out/` to track which files succeeded and which were lost due to timeouts.
